title: Nepal Flood Death Toll Surpasses 900 as Rescuers Race to Free Workers Trapped in Tunnels
excerpt: Rescue teams are using controlled blasts and airlifted excavators to reach an estimated 500 workers trapped in hydropower tunnels, while China rejects claims its Tibet projects triggered the disaster.
body:
• Nepal's death toll from last Wednesday's Himalayan floods has risen to 903, with 4,247 people still missing; combined deaths in Nepal and China have surpassed 950
  • Around 500 workers are believed trapped in hydropower tunnels across 11 projects in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, with rescue teams using controlled blasts and airlifted excavators to reach them
  • China rejected claims that its hydropower projects in Tibet triggered the disaster, calling such allegations "malicious speculation" and attributing the floods to a glacier collapse on Nepal's side
  • More than 80 Americans and 49 Indians are among over 800 foreign nationals unaccounted for on both sides of the Nepal-China border

Nepal's death toll from last Wednesday's catastrophic Himalayan floods climbed to 903 on Monday as rescue teams intensified efforts to reach hundreds of workers believed trapped inside mud-filled hydropower tunnels, while China dismissed allegations that its infrastructure projects in Tibet contributed to the disaster.

Tunnel Rescue Operations Intensify

The focus of Nepal's massive rescue effort — involving more than 20,000 army, police, and paramilitary personnel — has shifted to 11 hydropower projects in the hard-hit districts of Rasuwa and Nuwakot, where an estimated 933 workers remain unaccounted for. Of those, roughly 500 are believed to be trapped inside tunnels buried under dozens of feet of mud and debris.

https://x.com/AC360/status/2094496873595732249

The Nepali army said search-and-rescue teams used controlled blasts, excavators, and searchlights on Monday to clear water and mud to reach the trapped workers. At the Upper Trishuli 3A hydropower project in Nuwakot, army engineers conducted a controlled explosion at a tunnel entrance while two excavators airlifted to the location cleared debris at a depth of about 30 feet, according to the Wall Street Journal.

"A large amount of debris has been deposited and that is posing us a big challenge to open the tunnels. Our main focus is on opening the tunnels."

— Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet, Nepal Army spokesperson

On Sunday, a rescue team rappelled over a hole blasted into a section of another tunnel and called out but received no response from inside, the prime minister's office said. At a separate site, rescuers reached about 330 feet inside a tunnel only to find it completely blocked.

Six days after the disaster, fears are growing that some workers may have suffocated. Some had managed to make contact and call for help when the disaster struck, and others who escaped reported that many colleagues were still in the tunnels, said Mohan Kumar Dangi, president of the Independent Power Producers' Association, Nepal. Some 280 hydropower workers have been rescued so far, with tunnel experts from India, China, and South Korea assisting.

China Rejects Hydropower Link

As the disaster's scale became clearer, China pushed back against growing criticism linking its massive infrastructure projects in Tibet to the flooding. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun on Monday rejected claims that hydropower projects in Tibet contributed to the catastrophe, calling such allegations "malicious speculation that has no factual basis."

"According to their analysis, the mudslide was triggered by a collapse of a high-altitude glacier in Nepal," Guo said at a media briefing in Beijing. He also dismissed accusations that China was understating its casualty figures, saying search and rescue operations were continuing and information was being released "in an open and timely manner."

Scientists from the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development say the likely trigger was an ice-rock avalanche on the Langtang mountain range that temporarily dammed a tributary before bursting, sending a wall of ice, rock, and mud crashing through valley towns and across the border into China. Two Nepali officials told Reuters that China had not shared much information on glacier risks following an earlier meeting to strengthen cooperation, raising concerns about future disaster preparedness.

Mounting Toll and Missing Foreigners

Nepal's disaster management agency said 903 bodies had been recovered across the country, many found as far as 150 miles from where the flood originally struck. On the Chinese side, authorities reported 16 deaths in Gyirong County with 546 people missing. The combined death toll across both countries has surpassed 950.

Among the missing are more than 800 foreign nationals on both sides of the border — over 500 foreign tourists in Nepal and 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries unaccounted for in Tibet, according to Chinese authorities. Eighty Americans and 49 Indians are among those missing, many of them pilgrims visiting sacred lakes revered by Hindus and Buddhists. The Red Cross estimates more than 90,000 people have been affected.

Chinese President Xi Jinping, in Kyrgyzstan for a regional summit, said Monday that China is "sparing no effort" in the search for missing people. Nearly 100 Chinese citizens have not been contactable on the Nepalese side, Chinese officials said.

What Comes Next

Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah called the flood an "unprecedented and devastating natural disaster" and said more than 9,000 people had been evacuated, mainly by airlift. But risks persist: a lake formed across the Nepal-China border by the disaster could trigger fresh flooding after it began overflowing into Nepal's rivers, and China's state television reported Monday that glaciers around the impact crater remain at risk of further collapse.

The disaster has intensified scrutiny of Nepal's rapid expansion of hydropower infrastructure over the past decade, built to exploit steep Himalayan terrain for electricity generation. The country's tunnels, designed to carry water through mountains, became death traps when the debris-laden flood buried their openings under dozens of feet of mud.
image_caption: Rescue operations during the August 2026 Nepal floods, which have killed over 900 people with thousands still missing.
nri_angle: Eight Indian-origin U.S. nationals are among the missing, with 49 Indians unaccounted for on the Tibetan side and 80 Americans missing across both countries.
